 BREAKING: One-month-old baby dies after dog attack at Papillion home Children’s Nebraska doctors say e-ride injuries are up 400% in 3 years 
 Jessica Lee, program director for trauma and children’s surgery at Children’s Nebraska, said the effects reach the whole family. By Brenna Kiefner Published : Nov. 18, 2026 at 6:20 PM CST Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - Doctors at Children’s Nebraska say the wrong e-bike, scooter or e-moto can land a child in intensive care. They say parents considering one as a Christmas gift should check certain features before buying.
 Injuries doctors are seeing
 Doctors at Children’s Nebraska say they are seeing brain injuries, facial trauma that threatens a child’s airway and bones breaking through the skin from e-bikes, scooters and e-motos.
 They say injuries from the rides are up 400% in three years.
 Jessica Lee, program director for trauma and children’s surgery at Children’s Nebraska, said the effects reach the whole family.
 “A lot of the guilt that some of the parents and siblings are going through because they didn’t realize how dangerous that these e-rides are,” Lee said.
 Speed and learning curve
 Taylor Sterba, communications and outreach coordinator for Bike Walk Nebraska, said the difference between the devices is speed. She said a legal e-bike tops out at 28 mph, and anything faster is an e-moto.
 Sterba said the devices have a learning curve for parents and riders.
 “When parents aren’t accustomed to it, kids aren’t accustomed to it, they might just want to hit that brake. And if they’re going a certain speed, they might just go over the front of that device,” Sterba said.
 Why children want them
 Lindsey Button, a transportation planner with MAPA, said there is a reason children want the rides. In hilly Omaha, an electric-assist bike can help them get to school and to a friend’s house.
 “And they’re a lot more fun. But we want to make sure that folks are doing it safely and that they’re wearing the proper safety gear and that we’re not seeing the kinds of injuries that we’ve been seeing at Children’s,” Button said.
 What parents should check
 Children’s Nebraska, Bike Walk Nebraska and MAPA have a message for parents: make a list and check it twice.
 They say to look for working pedals, a top speed of 20 mph, and the right helmet and gear.
 Lee said those items can affect whether a child ends up in the hospital.
 “That is the part that can really impact whether a kid shows up here in our hospital or if they are able to go home that night,” Lee said.
